articles.title: Đổi mới vai trò người thầy trong kỷ nguyên AI: Từ truyền thụ tri thức đến kiến tạo năng lực
articles.text:
Đây là một vấn đề đáng suy ngẫm. Khi công nghệ có thể thay con người thực hiện một phần công việc, vai trò người thầy buộc phải dịch chuyển từ truyền thụ tri thức sang kiến tạo năng lực.
Từ chủ trương đến khung chính sách
Định hướng này bắt nguồn từ chủ trương nhất quán của Đảng. Nghị quyết số 71-NQ/TW ngày 22/8/2025 xác định rõ yêu cầu phổ cập, ứng dụng mạnh mẽ công nghệ số và trí tuệ nhân tạo trong dạy và học, chuyển tư duy giáo dục từ trang bị kiến thức sang phát triển năng lực người học. Phó Thủ tướng Lê Tiến Châu cụ thể hóa tinh thần đó: AI là công cụ hỗ trợ, không thay thế vai trò thầy cô, không làm thay năng lực người học.
Chủ trương này đang được thể chế hóa theo lộ trình bài bản, không nóng vội. Ngày 15/12/2025, Bộ Giáo dục và Đào tạo ban hành Quyết định số 3439/QĐ-BGDĐT về Khung nội dung thí điểm giáo dục AI cho học sinh phổ thông, gồm bốn mạch kiến thức: tư duy lấy con người làm trung tâm, đạo đức AI, kỹ thuật và ứng dụng, thiết kế hệ thống. Từ tháng 2/2026, việc thí điểm triển khai theo ba phương án: tích hợp vào môn học, dạy chủ đề độc lập, hoặc câu lạc bộ trải nghiệm; với hai đợt tập huấn cán bộ cốt cán trước khi nhân rộng đại trà. Cách làm "thí điểm trước, nhân rộng sau" cho thấy ngành giáo dục ý thức rõ rủi ro lệ thuộc công nghệ.
Bức tranh không chỉ ở một nơi
Việc thí điểm đang diễn ra ở nhiều địa phương theo điều kiện riêng. Tại TP Hồ Chí Minh, bốn nhóm trường chuyên, tiên tiến hội nhập, trường học số triển khai trước từ học kỳ II năm học 2025-2026. Tại Ninh Bình, Sở Giáo dục và Đào tạo ban hành kế hoạch thí điểm riêng, Trường THPT chuyên Biên Hòa là một trong những nơi đi đầu. Viện Khoa học Giáo dục Việt Nam trực tiếp thí điểm chương trình AI từ lớp 1 đến lớp 12 tại Trường Thực nghiệm Hà Nội. Ngay tại địa bàn khó khăn như Trường Phổ thông dân tộc bán trú Tiểu học Dào San (Lai Châu), giáo viên cũng đã sớm tiếp cận AI.
Cũng theo báo cáo TALIS 2024, 64,45% giáo viên Việt Nam đã ứng dụng AI trong giảng dạy, cao gấp đôi mức trung bình quốc tế. Một khảo sát khác của Viện Khoa học Giáo dục Việt Nam trên gần 35.000 giáo viên tại 44 tỉnh, thành cho kết quả tương tự: 76% từng dùng AI trong lớp học. Nhưng con số này đi kèm cảnh báo: gần 31% giáo viên vẫn phân vân về hiệu quả sử dụng, hơn 20% chưa thực sự tự tin. Nói cách khác, giáo viên Việt Nam không thiếu chủ động tiếp cận AI, nhưng phần lớn vẫn tự mày mò, thiếu khung năng lực và lộ trình đào tạo thống nhất.
Nguồn lực xã hội tham gia lấp khoảng trống
Trong lúc khung chính sách quốc gia đang hoàn thiện, một số cơ sở giáo dục ngoài công lập cũng chủ động đầu tư đào tạo AI, góp thêm nguồn lực xã hội.
Ở Hệ thống Phổ thông FPT, các trường ghi nhận một số cách làm đáng chú ý ở cấp độ từng giáo viên cho thấy khoảng trống về phương pháp đang được lấp đầy bằng chính sự chủ động của từng giáo viên. Tại Trường Tiểu học, THCS & THPT FPT Thanh Hóa, cô Đặng Thị Hương, giáo viên Toán đã dùng AI tạo nhân vật hoạt hình đồng hành cùng học sinh lớp 2 trong mỗi tiết học, giúp hơn 90% học sinh phản hồi tích cực về mức độ hứng thú sau một học kỳ. Tại FPT School Hậu Giang, thầy Lê Hữu Kỳ Quan, giáo viên Tin học kiêm Tổ trưởng Tổ Khoa học Tự nhiên cùng giáo viên Vovinam đã hợp tác đưa AI vào nhận diện đúng, sai của từng thế võ để học sinh tự luyện tập. Ở bậc đại học, Trường ĐH FPT mở lớp tập huấn AI cho học sinh, giáo viên THPT ở các địa phương lân cận, vừa tái cấu trúc chương trình đào tạo để năng lực làm chủ công nghệ trở thành yêu cầu chung cho mọi ngành học.
Ở một hệ thống giáo dục tư nhân khác như EQuest từ năm học 2025-2026 đã triển khai đồng loạt phòng AI, STEM Lab xuyên suốt các cấp học, xác định năng lực AI là kỹ năng nền tảng bắt buộc.
Đây là hướng đi mà nhiều cơ sở giáo dục đại học, cả công lập lẫn tư thục, đang từng bước theo đuổi khi thị trường lao động dịch chuyển nhanh dưới tác động của AI.
Những mô hình như vậy đều có điểm chung: xuất phát từ sự chủ động của cơ sở giáo dục, không chờ chính sách hoàn thiện mới bắt đầu, đúng tinh thần xã hội hóa giáo dục mà Nghị quyết 71-NQ/TW đề ra.
AI giải phóng người thầy, không thay thế người thầy
Khi giáo viên chủ động làm chủ AI dù ở một trường công lập tại Ninh Bình, một trường thực nghiệm ở Hà Nội, hay một trường tư thục, công nghệ trở thành công cụ giúp họ thoát khỏi những phần việc lặp đi lặp lại, để dành thời gian cho những việc chỉ con người mới làm được: truyền cảm hứng, rèn tư duy phản biện, bồi dưỡng năng khiếu riêng của từng học sinh.
Nói cách khác, AI không đe dọa nghề giáo, ở bất kỳ loại hình trường nào. Nó chỉ đặt ra một yêu cầu buộc người thầy và cả người quản lý giáo dục phải trả lời: sẵn sàng học cách làm chủ công cụ mới, để dành trọn thời gian và nguồn lực còn lại cho sứ mệnh mà không công nghệ nào thay thế được.

articles.title: The Absolute Pleasure of Tim Curry
articles.text:
The Absolute Pleasure of Tim Curry
His magic lay in his ability to be outrageous without being self-conscious.
It’s a brisk night in downtown Boston in the early 1980s, and I’m out with a group that includes a very nice, very pretty young woman from my college whom I hope to get to know better. After dinner, one of the guys has an idea: a movie! Better yet, a midnight movie, after which, of course, we’d have to be gallant and walk the girls home. Ambling down Newbury Street to the Exeter Street Theater (now long gone), I spot an unexpected and sartorially strange crowd lined up around the corner. I am dressed like a basic preppy-wannabe: jeans, loafers, a button-down shirt. But the people lined up to get into this movie include men in heavy makeup and—wait, can this be?—garter belts. What the hell am I doing here?
The movie, of course, was the 1975 flop turned cult hit The Rocky Horror Picture Show, and audiences came dressed as their favorite character. Those tarted-up men were paying tribute to Tim Curry’s bizarrely glorious Dr. Frank-N-Furter, who belts out a song about being a “sweet transvestite from Transsexual, Transylvania.” I may have been a youthful Republican, but I knew that I was watching something—and someone—amazing. I saw the movie many more times, and although I wasn’t going in drag (if you know Rocky Horror, I was more the Brad Majors type), Curry’s pure, perverse joy on-screen was always a welcome escape.
The English actor died today at 80. In a perfect tribute, Curry’s many fans are happily debating his greatest performances, which is remarkable given that he wasn’t in that many films and was rarely the lead. Yet his charisma ensured a loyal following for generations.
Finding Curry in something was always a treat. But it was particularly special for me, as someone who worked in Russian affairs, when I discovered that he had traded his pumps and pearls for the severe tunic of a Soviet naval officer in The Hunt for Red October. Curry played the clueless medical officer Dr. Petrov, who does not realize that his skipper, Captain Ramius (played by Sean Connery), intends to defect to the West. When Ramius appears to valiantly order Petrov off the boat and says that, as captain, he himself must go down with the ship after “fighting” the Americans, Curry, trembling with admiration, says, “You’ll receive the Order of Lenin for this, Captain.” His is a simple line, but Curry’s combination of posh earnestness and wide-eyed gullibility turns this into a gem of a moment, something that only he could pull off.
What was it about Curry that endeared him to so many? Unlike Dolly Parton, who is rightly being mourned as a great American, Curry was far less a public person. He never married. Despite playing the most decadent and flamboyant cross-dresser in the history of cinema, he never answered questions about his sexuality or his personal relationships. (“Respectfully,” he wrote in his 2025 memoir, such things are “none of your fucking business.”) He was known to be a charming and warm man, and he was involved with some charity efforts, but despite his extroversion as a performer, he was not an off-screen supernova.
Instead, Curry connected with fans like me because, as a performer, the man seemed able to do anything, and do it with a kind of liberated abandon and eagerness to entertain. (He said later that he put so much energy into his performance in Clue that the nurse on set warned him that he was at risk of having a heart attack.) A prancing, snide alien in women’s underwear who talks like an upper-class London lord? Sure, he could do that. How about an exuberant and hilarious turn as Long John Silver with a cast of Muppets? Of course. And as a Russian villain in the dreadful remake of McHale’s Navy, he single-handedly made the movie (or at least some of it) worth watching.
His distinctive voice and knack for accents also ensured him gigs in cartoons and video games, including as the Soviet premier Cherdenko in the alternate-history video game Command & Conquer: Red Alert 3. (What was it with him and Russians?) Many famous actors have appeared in video games, but with uneven results; instead of phoning it in, Curry joined the small band of stars who acted in video games and elevated what could have been throwaway scenes into memorably fun mini-movies.
Curry’s gifts usually made more of an impression on audiences than on film critics, and most of his award nominations were for stage roles. Yet his rich voice and easy charm lent even the cheesiest lines a kind of Shakespearian seriousness, and watching him was like having an expensive meal and comfort food at the same time. Maybe that’s what was so appealing about Curry: He was a guilty pleasure, but without the guilt. You knew you were watching a great actor, regardless of the script.
Curry always seemed to be having a great time in every role, and he seemed to want audiences to have a great time too. As Frank-N-Furter would say, “There’s no crime in giving yourself over to pleasure.” When Tim Curry was on-screen, nothing was easier.

articles.title: An Giang: Đội K92 quy tập 63 hài cốt liệt sĩ từ ấp rẫy Mới, xã Kiên Lương
articles.text:
Ngày 26/8, thượng tá Nguyễn Thanh Hùng, Đội trưởng Đội K92, Bộ CHQS tỉnh An Giang cho biết, đơn vị tiếp tục tìm kiếm được thêm một hài cốt liệt sĩ tại khu vực ấp Rẫy Mới, xã Kiên Lương.
Ngay sau khi phát hiện, cán bộ, chiến sĩ Đội K92 thận trọng thu gom từng phần hài cốt, kiểm tra các di vật liên quan; đồng thời ghi nhận vị trí, đặc điểm mộ và những thông tin tại hiện trường phục vụ công tác xác minh.
Từ vị trí vừa phát hiện, đơn vị tiếp tục mở rộng phạm vi, rà soát kỹ lớp đất xung quanh nhằm không bỏ sót hài cốt và di vật của các liệt sĩ.
Sau khi quy tập được hài cốt liệt sĩ, lực lượng làm nhiệm vụ đã hoàn trả lại mặt bằng cho khu vực đã đào.
Thượng tá Nguyễn Thanh Hùng cho biết, tính đến ngày 26/8 (giai đoạn XXVI (2026 - 2027)), Đội K92 đã tìm kiếm, quy tập được 70 bộ hài cốt liệt sĩ, trong đó 63 bộ được quy tập tại ấp Rẫy Mới, xã Kiên Lương.
"Việc tìm kiếm được 63 hài cốt liệt sĩ tại khu vực ấp Rẫy Mới là kết quả rất quan trọng. Chúng tôi xác định còn thông tin, còn dấu hiệu thì còn tổ chức tìm kiếm, từng vị trí đều được kiểm tra kỹ, với quyết tâm cao nhất đưa các liệt sĩ trở về nhà", ông Hùng chia sẻ.

articles.title: Economists Who Weren’t Worried About the Debt Are Now Panicking
articles.text:
Economists Who Weren’t Worried About the Debt Are Now Panicking
What really concerns them isn’t just the $40 trillion.
This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here.
America’s national debt hit $40 trillion last week. That number certainly feels like something worth panicking over—the mind balks at all the zeros. But although the debt has been in the trillions for decades, not everyone has considered it a problem.
One camp of economists has been warning about the perils of high debt for years: Budget hawks predicted that if the country kept spending and didn’t raise taxes enough to keep pace, the resulting fiscal crisis could be devastating. But others—the doves—have brushed it off. Their perspective was that as long as the U.S. GDP was growing faster than the interest rate it was paying on its debt, the Treasury would be able to keep rolling over its bonds without too much of a problem. For much of the 2010s, this was essentially the status quo, and debt panic was muted.
We’re nowhere near a complete failure of the Treasury market, and yet, over the past couple of years, some economists who were once more dovish have switched teams. Martha Gimbel, the executive director of the Budget Lab at Yale and the author of a recent Atlantic story on this issue, told me that part of the reason these economists are pivoting is that they’re starting to realize that interest rates are “probably going to be elevated for quite some time.” The average interest rate on U.S. debt—that second variable the doves look at—has been relatively high for several years now, and it’s only growing. It was hovering around 1.5 percent in 2021, and it’s now roughly 3.4 percent. The yield on the 30-year Treasury bond has more than doubled since 2021. “I was not a deficit hawk, and that reflected the dynamics” of the 2010s, when rates were lower, Gimbel told me. Now, she said, “the environment has changed.”
Why are rates rising? The Fed’s reaction to inflation is one reason. It may also have something to do with the extreme investments being made in AI, and these companies’ demand for credit. And it’s likely connected to the deficit panic—concern about the expansion of the national debt and the government’s ability to sustain it. Investors are starting to think of long-term Treasurys as riskier than they once did, and they’re demanding more money in exchange for taking on America’s debt. At the same time, the federal government has shown no real appetite to pull its two main levers for reducing the debt: cutting spending and raising taxes.
Jared Bernstein, the former head of Joe Biden’s Council of Economic Advisers, wrote in The Atlantic a few months ago that he’d “flipped from dove to hawk”—and told me this week that it was partly the government’s complacency on this issue that spurred this change. “Neither side seems particularly motivated to do much of anything about this,” he said. Rather than attending to the debt problem, politicians of both parties have instituted major tax cuts and increased spending over the past 25 years. The U.S. had its credit downgraded by a major ratings agency last spring, in part because of rising debt. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act will add an estimated $4.7 trillion to the deficit through 2035, and Donald Trump’s efforts to decrease immigration will add another half a trillion to that number over the same period, per the Congressional Budget Office.
Despite some recent attempts at short-term stabilization, his administration hasn’t done much to assure the country’s creditors that everything’s fine; they now appear to be seeking greater yields as a result. When longer-term bond yields rise, as they have been, everyday forms of borrowing such as mortgage rates and student loans tend to become more expensive as well. That’s why yields are ultimately “a kitchen-table issue in the same way that inflation is,” Ernie Tedeschi, a former chief economist for the White House’s Council of Economic Advisers, told me.
Last week, in an apparent attempt to depress yields, the Treasury Department announced that it would be more than doubling the size of its longer-term-bond buybacks. It worked briefly—yields fell—but about 24 hours later, they climbed higher than where they were before. In a scathing (and AI-written) Wall Street Journal op-ed this week, the investor and longtime deficit hawk Stanley Druckenmiller, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent’s former mentor, stressed that the increased buybacks were a distraction from the real problem: the government’s spending.
This political inertia likely stems from the fact that the two most important levers for reducing the debt—raising taxes and cutting spending—remain unpopular among lawmakers and voters alike. Bessent suggested last week that he’s interested in a third option: stimulating the economy enough that it once again outpaces interest rates. But without a concrete plan in place, this sounds like wishful thinking, especially when the more obvious solutions to fix the deficit remain untapped. “This is the era of ‘No tax on blank’ in our politics right now,” Tedeschi said. On the campaign trail, Trump promised to remove taxes on tips, overtime pay, and Social Security payments; he accomplished the first and second, and took steps toward the third. That’s “exactly the opposite mentality we need to have if we want to stabilize our debt going forward,” Tedeschi said.
Likelier than a true collapse of the Treasury market, he told me, is that both the debt and interest rates keep rising over time, and that “the days of the 2 or low 3 percent mortgage of a few years ago are just gone.” With affordability concerns playing a major role in the midterms, politicians aren’t exactly clamoring to raise taxes on their constituents. But affordability is exactly what’s at stake if Washington doesn’t at least attempt to chip away at the debt problem.
Related:
Here are four new stories from The Atlantic:
Today’s News
- Flash floods swept through parts of Nepal and Tibet, killing more than 150 people in Nepal; hundreds remain missing across the region. Nepal and China have declared emergencies and launched rescue efforts.
- Meta agreed to pay about $18 billion to settle lawsuits from states claiming that its platforms harmed young users. The company did not admit wrongdoing but has agreed to changes, including daily time limits for teen users.
- A coalition of Democratic-led states sued the Trump administration over new Postal Service rules affecting voting by mail. The lawsuit follows Monday’s Supreme Court ruling allowing the administration to move forward with its plans to restrict voting by mail while legal challenges continue.
Evening Read
The Most Beautiful Woman
By Annie Joy Williams
Growing up in Tennessee, I could hardly walk into a grocery store without hearing “Jolene” playing on the radio. My mom sang fragments of “9 to 5” as she cooked Hamburger Helper on school nights, after clocking out of work. At my babysitter’s house in the summer, where Country Music Television was our ambient noise, she’d shout, “Good golly, Miss Dolly!” every time a Dolly song came on (which was at least every 30 minutes). Dolly Parton was more of an institution than a star to Tennesseans. Her image was plastered on T-shirts and hung on walls, like Mother Mary would be in a Catholic home. We vacationed at her amusement park, Dollywood, every school break. No one ever used her last name—she was simply Dolly to us all, and she was living proof that tough odds were no match for a cup of ambition.
When Dolly’s death was announced yesterday afternoon, my phone lit up with texts from hometown friends. “It feels like a member of our family died in Tennessee today,” one friend said. My socialist sister said Tennessee’s poet laureate had left us. My Donald Trump–voting father cried. In Tennessee, whether you fly a MAGA flag or a Pride flag, one thing is for sure: You’re listening to Dolly.

articles.title: iPhone 18 Pro có thể tạo bước nhảy lớn nhờ chip 2nm
articles.text:
Theo Analytics Insight, iPhone 18 Pro và 18 Pro Max có thể là một trong những đợt nâng cấp phần cứng đáng chú ý của Apple trong vài năm gần đây. Thay vì tập trung vào thay đổi mạnh ngoại hình, hãng được cho là tập trung vào chip, camera, màn hình, kết nối và thời lượng pin.
Chip 2nm có thể là nâng cấp lớn nhất
Thay đổi đáng chú ý nhất được dự báo nằm ở A20 Pro, chip thế hệ mới dành cho dòng iPhone Pro.
Chip A20 Pro có khả năng được sản xuất trên tiến trình 2nm của TSMC, thay cho công nghệ 3nm đang được sử dụng trên thế hệ trước. Một số báo cáo ước tính chip mới có thể tăng hiệu năng khoảng 15-18%, trong khi hiệu quả sử dụng năng lượng cải thiện khoảng 30%.
A20 Pro còn được cho là có thể sử dụng công nghệ đóng gói WMCM (Wafer-Level Multi-Chip Module). Cách thiết kế này cho phép đặt bộ nhớ RAM gần CPU, GPU và Neural Engine hơn, qua đó rút ngắn đường truyền dữ liệu và hạn chế năng lượng thất thoát.
Nếu được áp dụng, thay đổi không chỉ phục vụ tốc độ xử lý thông thường mà còn có thể tác động tới những tác vụ trí tuệ nhân tạo chạy trực tiếp trên thiết bị - lĩnh vực ngày càng đòi hỏi khả năng trao đổi dữ liệu nhanh giữa CPU, GPU, bộ nhớ và bộ xử lý AI.
Dynamic Island nhỏ hơn, Face ID có thể xuống dưới màn hình.
Kích thước màn hình của hai phiên bản Pro được dự báo không thay đổi nhiều. iPhone 18 Pro có thể tiếp tục sử dụng màn hình khoảng 6,3 inch, trong khi Pro Max khoảng 6,9 inch.
Điểm khác biệt nằm ở khu vực phía trên màn hình. Nhiều báo cáo cho rằng Apple đang tìm cách thu nhỏ Dynamic Island bằng việc đưa một số thành phần của hệ thống Face ID xuống dưới tấm nền.
Nếu thành hiện thực, đây sẽ là một bước tiếp theo trong quá trình Apple thu hẹp phần khuyết màn hình trên iPhone, giúp tăng diện tích hiển thị mà không cần tăng kích thước tổng thể của thiết bị.
Tuy nhiên, kích thước Dynamic Island cũng như cấu trúc Face ID cuối cùng chưa được hãng công bố.
Camera khẩu độ biến thiên lần đầu xuất hiện trên iPhone? Camera được dự báo là thay đổi dễ nhận thấy nhất đối với người dùng.
Các thế hệ iPhone Pro hiện sử dụng camera chính với khẩu độ cố định. Trong khi đó, iPhone 18 Pro được cho là có thể chuyển sang khẩu độ biến thiên cơ học, cho phép điều chỉnh lượng ánh sáng đi qua ống kính.
Cơ chế này giúp camera thích ứng tốt hơn với nhiều điều kiện ánh sáng và kiểm soát độ sâu trường ảnh. Trong môi trường sáng, khẩu độ có thể thu nhỏ; khi thiếu sáng, hệ thống có thể mở khẩu lớn hơn để thu nhận nhiều ánh sáng.
Khẩu độ biến thiên cũng có khả năng hỗ trợ quay video khi điều kiện ánh sáng thay đổi liên tục, giúp quá trình chuyển đổi phơi sáng tự nhiên hơn.
Dù vậy, một số nguồn tin cho rằng Apple có thể chỉ trang bị công nghệ này trên iPhone 18 Pro Max, trong khi bản Pro tiếp tục sử dụng khẩu độ cố định.
Phiên bản Pro Max còn được đồn đoán có khả năng nâng zoom quang học lên 6x với hệ thống lăng kính, nhưng thông tin này hiện có mức độ xác thực thấp hơn so với các báo cáo về khẩu độ biến thiên.
Apple muốn tự kiểm soát nhiều linh kiện cốt lõi hơn
Một thay đổi khác được nhắc đến là modem C2 do Apple phát triển. Chip này được kỳ vọng cải thiện hiệu quả sử dụng năng lượng và khả năng kết nối mạng di động, đồng thời thể hiện chiến lược đưa ngày càng nhiều linh kiện quan trọng trên iPhone về hệ sinh thái phần cứng do Apple kiểm soát.
Một số nguồn còn đề cập khả năng hỗ trợ kết nối 5G qua vệ tinh, song chưa có đủ bằng chứng để khẳng định tính năng này sẽ xuất hiện trên sản phẩm thương mại.
Apple cũng có thể nâng cấp chip kết nối không dây từ N1 lên thế hệ N2. Những cải tiến ở chip và modem đồng thời có thể tác động trực tiếp đến thời lượng pin. A20 Pro với tiến trình 2 nm được kỳ vọng tiêu thụ ít điện hơn, trong khi iPhone 18 Pro Max được đồn đoán trang bị pin dung lượng lớn hơn.
Một nguồn ước tính viên pin của Pro Max có thể đạt 5.567 mAh, nguồn khác cho rằng dung lượng tăng khoảng 10% so với thế hệ trước.
Điểm đáng chú ý của iPhone 18 Pro có thể không nằm ở một thiết kế hoàn toàn mới, mà ở cách Apple thay đổi cấu trúc phần cứng bên trong: từ tiến trình sản xuất chip, đóng gói bộ nhớ, camera đến modem.
Nguồn tin cũng cho rằng Apple có thể thay đổi lịch trình giới thiệu iPhone. Các mẫu iPhone 18 Pro, Pro Max và thiết bị màn hình gập có khả năng xuất hiện trong tháng 9/ 2026, trong khi iPhone 18 tiêu chuẩn và iPhone 18e có thể được chuyển sang nửa đầu năm 2027.
iPhone 18 Pro có thể không cần một thiết kế mới để đánh dấu một bước tiến lớn. Sản phẩm được sản xuất trên tiến trình 2nm.Chip A20 ProMột thiết kế mô-đun chip mới, Dynamic Island nhỏ hơn, khẩu độ camera thay đổi và modem C2 của Apple có thể thay đổi cách điện thoại xử lý các tác vụ khó khăn nhất.
Apple cũng có thể chia đợt ra mắt iPhone 18 thành hai giai đoạn, với các mẫu Pro và thiết bị gập vào mùa thu năm 2026, trong khi iPhone 18 tiêu chuẩn và iPhone 18e được cho là sẽ ra mắt vào nửa đầu năm 2027.
Những thay đổi lớn nhất có thể nằm bên trong con chip, phía sau các camera và bên dưới màn hình. Với mẫu mới này Apple có thể tạo ra cảm giác mới mẻ cho iPhone 18 Pro thông qua việc điều khiển phần cứng chứ không phải bằng một hình dáng bên ngoài mới.

articles.title: How to Lose $12 Billion and Still Win
articles.text:
Meta avoided the worst today by settling a massive lawsuit over alleged damages “to the mental and physical wellbeing of America’s youth.” The case, brought by the attorneys general of 47 states, plus U.S. territories and Washington, D.C., had been mid-trial in a federal court in California and was by far the most significant legal challenge the company has ever faced. To resolve the lawsuit, Meta will have to make a slew of design changes to its social-media platforms, and it will pay more than $12 billion—down from the approximately $200 billion that was initially sought, and a fraction of the $60 billion that the company made in profit last year.
The settlement can be used by the states and other parties to pay for their litigation costs and for a variety of school and community programs. Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers agreed to the proposal this morning, saying “I’m quite happy” and congratulating both parties. There seems to be good cheer all around; Meta, which avoided any admission of guilt, put out a sunny announcement framing the agreement as part of its “longstanding efforts to empower parents and support teens.” Brian Schwalb, the attorney general of the District of Columbia, told The New York Times that the settlement represents a “monumental public health victory” that will “fundamentally and immediately change how young people use Instagram and Facebook.”
The former claim will have to be proved over time, but the latter is clearly true. As part of the agreement, Meta has agreed to submit to regular auditing of both its age-verification systems and its efforts to prevent minors from making multiple accounts to get around its restrictions. And the company will make other tweaks that are intended to target the big recent villains of social media: short-form video and the never-ending feed.
Teen users, by default, will not have access to most features of Instagram and Facebook at night (though they can still access messages and settings) and will not receive notifications from the platforms during school hours (defined as 8 a.m. to 3 p.m. on weekdays from August 15 to June 15). They’ll also be limited to a maximum of one hour a day per platform, though this doesn’t include time spent sending messages or consuming long-form content (which the agreement defines as audio or video at least 22 minutes long). Meta is also required to interrupt scrolling every 15 minutes with pop-ups that encourage “productive pauses,” and the company will have to study how well the interruptions work and submit its findings to an auditor. Parents can still manually change any of these settings for their kids.
The settlement also requires limits on features that some experts believe are detrimental to teenagers’ self-esteem and self-image. By default, teen users won’t see the number of likes or reactions on posts; they also won’t be able to use “cosmetic procedure filters,” which have been a sore spot for Meta for some time. When the plaintiffs filed their complaint, they cited evidence that Mark Zuckerberg had personally vetoed a proposed in-house policy against these filters despite concerns expressed by employees that they were causing young people to develop body dysmorphia. Meta will also be legally required to maintain and enforce the “age-appropriate” content guidelines it debuted at the end of last year.
This may seem like quite a lot of changes—especially considering that the case is not even the end of Meta’s legal problems. The company is still facing numerous lawsuits filed by individuals and school districts. “If Meta is going to resolve all its pending liabilities, this is only the first of several large checks it is going to have to write,” Eric Goldman, a professor at Santa Clara University School of Law, told me. But today’s settlement shows that the tech company was able to “buy out one of the most serious legal threats” it faced, and it managed to do so without acquiescing to demands that might have been truly destructive to its business. Meta will have to give teen users the ability to opt in to a chronological, non-personalized feed, but the company does not have to pivot away from the default algorithmic recommendations that many critics characterize as addictive. It seems unlikely that many people will select a straightforward chronological feed; Meta has tested this change before and found that users did not like it.
As for the one-hour limit, in an email, a Meta spokesperson told me that the average American teenager spends about 66 minutes a day on Instagram anyway, and that teen activity across platforms accounts for less than 1 percent of the company’s revenue. So perhaps these were battles that the company could afford to lose.
The attorneys general “made a bunch of guesses” as to what kinds of changes might help kids, Goldman said, and have pulled off a major success in getting Meta to accept them. Many of these interventions might have suffered First Amendment challenges if they’d been pursued by other methods. (For instance, if the plaintiffs had actually won at trial.) Mark Bartholomew, a professor at the University at Buffalo School of Law, agreed, writing to me that “the state AGs got Meta to consent to dramatic limits on its own speech that Congress was unlikely to go for and the courts were unlikely to bless.”
The company is now promoting the changes widely and calling on other social-media platforms to follow suit. It has also agreed to pay an additional $5.3 billion if TikTok and YouTube, which are also defendants in the ongoing litigation, implement restrictions and pay into the settlement. Although this is not the end of Meta’s legal battles—personal-injury lawsuits similar to the one it lost in March will likely keep coming—the company has won the opportunity to select its own restrictions, define its own limits, and discard its own deal-breakers, effectively setting a standard that the rest of the industry will be expected to abide by without having had any say in its creation.
“Obviously, Meta doesn’t want to unilaterally disarm in the war for user attention while its rivals are allowed to continue,” Bartholomew noted. At the start of the year, when the first of Meta’s big cases came to trial, I wrote that social media had come to a fork in the road: The lawsuits were asking existential questions about whether social-media platforms are responsible for a mental-health crisis and whether it is possible to hold them accountable for it. This agreement answers only the second question—yes, it is possible, but for now, it may be possible on only one company’s terms.

articles.title: Nghệ An: Phạt nguội qua camera 60 thanh, thiếu niên vi phạm giao thông lúc "đi bão"
articles.text:
Chiều 26/8, thông tin từ Phòng Cảnh sát Giao thông (Công an tỉnh Nghệ An) cho biết: Đơn vị vừa lập biên bản vi phạm hành chính với hàng chục thanh thiếu niên vi phạm các quy định của pháp luật khi tham gia giao thông trong đêm chung kết lượt đi ASEAN Cup 2026 giữa đội tuyển Việt Nam với Thái Lan.
Theo đó, tối 22/8 vừa qua đã diễn ra trận chung kết lượt đi ASEAN Cup 2026 giữa đội tuyển Việt Nam - Thái Lan. Kết quả, tuyển Việt Nam dành chiến thắng 2-0.
Sau trận đấu, tại Nghệ An, đông đảo người dân mang theo cờ Tổ quốc, trống, kèn đổ ra các tuyến đường trung tâm, xung quanh Quảng trường Hồ Chí Minh, như: Trường Thi, Hồ Tùng Mậu, Nguyễn Văn Cừ, Trần Phú, Lê Mao, Lê Duẩn… để hòa chung không khí ăn mừng chiến thắng.
Bên cạnh những người dân tuân thủ Luật trật tự, an toàn giao thông thì vẫn có một số thanh, thiếu niên lợi dụng việc cổ vũ, ăn mừng chiến thắng, điều khiển xe mô tô tụ tập, chạy thành đoàn với tốc độ cao, không đội mũ bảo hiểm… tiềm ẩn nguy cơ gây tai nạn và mất an ninh, trật tự.
Trước tình hình trên, Ban Giám đốc Công an tỉnh Nghệ An đã chỉ đạo Phòng Cảnh sát giao thông triển khai lực lượng Cảnh sát giao thông và Tổ công tác 1354 thực hiện biện pháp bảo đảm an ninh, trật tự, an toàn giao thông, tạo điều kiện để người dân ăn mừng chiến thắng trong an toàn, văn minh.
Bên cạnh công tác tuần tra, kiểm soát, lực lượng chức năng đã sử dụng hệ thống camera ghi nhận hình ảnh các trường hợp vi phạm, phục vụ công tác xác minh, xử lý, trong đó có việc xử phạt nguội theo quy định.
Kết quả, đơn vị đã lập biên bản vi phạm hành chính 60 trường hợp, tạm giữ 30 xe mô tô, với các lỗi vi phạm như: không có giấy phép lái xe, không đội mũ bảo hiểm, chở quá số người quy định, tự ý thay đổi hình dáng, kết cấu xe, người chưa đủ tuổi điều khiển xe mô tô, xe gắn máy...
Hiện Phòng Cảnh sát giao thông Công an Nghệ An đang hoàn tất hồ sơ để xử lý các trường hợp vi phạm.
Cũng theo Phòng Cảnh sát giao thông trong tối nay 26/8, lực lượng Cảnh sát giao thông các địa phương, đặc biệt là địa bàn các phường đô thị Vinh để tập trung xử lý các trường hợp vi phạm TTATGT. Lực lượng chức năng cũng tăng cường sử dụng các biện pháp nghiệp vụ, trong đó có ghi hình phạt nguội các vi phạm.

articles.title: Hậu vệ Nguyễn Thành Chung hôn vợ trên sân Mỹ Đình
articles.text:
TPO - Trong giây phút đội tuyển Việt Nam ăn mừng chiến thắng vô địch ASEAN Cup 2026, hậu vệ Nguyễn Thành Chung gây chú ý khi hôn vợ - hot girl Ngô Tố Uyên.
Sau màn trao cúp vô địch và huy chương vàng, các cầu thủ tuyển bóng đá quốc gia Việt Nam tranh thủ chụp ảnh lưu lại những khoảnh đáng nhớ.
Người nhà xuống sân chúc mừng hậu vệ Nguyễn Thành Chung.Hậu vệ người Tuyên Quang không ngần ngại hôn vợ, hot girl Ngô Tố Uyên, trên sân Mỹ Đình. Nguyễn Thành Chung và vợ kết hôn vào năm 2022 ở Hà Nội. Họ có hai con trai. Tố Uyên được nhận xét là nàng WAG có ngoại hình đẹp nhất nhì Việt Nam.Văn Hậu ôm con trai sau trận thắng. Trước giờ bóng lăn, bố mẹ cùng vợ con đều có mặt tại sân Mỹ Đình để cổ vũ cho cầu thủ sinh năm 1999. Anh và người đẹp Doãn Hải Mỹ kết hôn năm 2023. Một năm sau, họ chào đón con trai đầu lòng, bé Đoàn Minh Đăng.Lê Phạm Thành Long tận hưởng giây phút chiến thắng bên hai con. Đây sẽ là khoảnh khắc để đời của cả ba cha con.
HLV Kim Sang-sik và các học trò rạng rỡ bên cúp vàng. Họ cùng nhau bảo vệ thành công danh hiệu nhà vô địch ASEAN Cup giành được từ năm 2024.
Quang Hải, Đình Bắc và các đồng đội không bỏ lỡ cơ hội được chụp ảnh cùng cúp vô địch. Họ đã có mùa thi đấu rực rỡ, nỗ lực trong những tháng qua và được đền đáp xứng đáng bằng thành tích hiện tại.
Nhà cầm quân đến từ Hàn Quốc được các cầu thủ tung lên cao, thay cho lời tri ân đã dẫn dắt tuyển quốc gia mang lại vinh quang cho đất nước.
Các cầu thủ lưu giữ lại khoảnh khắc đáng nhớ bên cúp vàng và HLV Kim Sang-sik.
Hoàng Hên đội nón lá, giơ cao quốc kỳ Việt Nam ăn mừng chiến thắng. 2026 là năm đáng nhớ trong sự nghiệp của anh khi lần đầu được triệu tập lên đội tuyển quốc gia Việt Nam.Xuân Son không quên lá cờ đỏ sao vàng trong khoảnh khắc đáng tự hào này. Sau ASEAN Cup 2024, anh gặp chấn thương nghiêm trọng và mất nhiều thời gian để hồi phục. Thành tích ấn tượng tại mùa giải 2026 giúp anh tái khẳng định vị thế hàng đầu Đông Nam Á.Tiền đạo Xuân Son ôm thủ môn Patrik Lê Giang. Hai người đều thể hiện xuất sắc trong cả mùa giải. Dù không ghi bàn trong trận cuối cùng, Xuân Son vẫn "bỏ túi" 5 bàn thắng. Patrik chứng minh giá trị bản thân bằng những pha cản bóng nghẹt thở.

articles.title: Why Did John Ratcliffe Go to Moscow?
articles.text:
Why Did John Ratcliffe Go to Moscow?
Despite Trump’s claims, the CIA director’s visit was anything but routine. It might be a sign that Putin is getting more dangerous.
CIA Director John Ratcliffe’s brief trip to Moscow yesterday was unannounced but hard to miss: He flew in a C-17A, a large heavy-transport plane, that open-source analysts quickly identified and tracked. Within hours, he was already on his way home.
The purpose of Ratcliffe’s visit remains unknown. In an interview with Glenn Beck this morning, President Trump described it as “sort of semi-routine,” but such trips are rare. The previous time a director of the CIA went to Russia was in November 2021, when William J. Burns told Moscow that the United States knew of Vladimir Putin’s plans to invade Ukraine. A likelier explanation for this latest trip is that Russia is getting more dangerous and the Trump administration wanted to warn it against escalating.
Ratcliffe’s visit comes at one of the most difficult periods in the war for the Kremlin. Thanks to its drone systems, Ukraine has been able to strike military targets and oil infrastructure deep inside Russia while also hindering Moscow’s advance on the battlefield, turning the front into a kill box in which anything that moves is struck within minutes. Despite making little progress, Russia has continued to take heavy losses. In May, the Russian death toll reached nearly half a million, according to Anne Keast-Butler, the head of GCHQ, the U.K. intelligence agency.
Russia’s weakness could be making Putin more reckless. The Wall Street Journal reported a few weeks ago that the U.S. intelligence community is concerned that Russia could carry out a limited attack on a NATO state, possibly even launching a small land incursion. Such an assault might thwart Russia’s own interests, prompting Europe to accelerate its military buildup and target Moscow’s sovereign assets. But Putin may see attacking a NATO country as an unprecedented opportunity to break the alliance, by manufacturing a crisis in which the United States fails to act.
If Washington did not respond to such an act of aggression, Russia could expose NATO’s mutual-protection clause as hollow. Putin has some reason to think that the United States may stay out of a conflict if he initiates one soon. Trump has repeatedly expressed disdain for Europe and shown little interest in challenging Putin. In addition, America’s weapons stockpile is depleted from the Iran war. Perhaps in response to fears of increased Russian aggression, NATO mounted a large U.S.-led air exercise last week over Poland and the Baltic region, which included flights near the Russian enclave of Kaliningrad.
Other possible signs of Putin’s growing belligerence have emerged. In recent weeks, a series of low-level attacks have swept Europe. Drones laden with explosives were found at the Leipzig airport this month, and there were explosions or fires at weapons factories and other sensitive sites in Estonia, Italy, Bulgaria, and the Netherlands, all of which have provided assistance to Ukraine. Authorities have attributed some but not all of the attacks to Moscow, and Russian officials have denied responsibility. But they follow an established pattern of Russian provocations in Europe.
Regardless of Putin’s ambitions elsewhere in Europe, he appears committed to fight the war in Ukraine indefinitely. Russia has increased its ballistic-missile attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure, taking advantage of Kyiv’s shortages in air defense. Reporting from the Journal suggests that Putin could be preparing a large-scale mobilization to replenish Russia’s army for a renewed offensive. The Russian leader might try to overwhelm Ukraine this winter with a massive bombardment campaign aimed at destroying its energy grid. But Kyiv is unlikely to capitulate, because it knows that Putin would impose punitive terms.
If Ukraine does survive the winter and retains the ability to strike deep inside of Russia, then Putin might choose to end the war in mid-2027. Facing the prospect of a U.S. president in 2029 who is more pro-Ukraine than Trump is, Putin may opt to take a favorable deal from this administration. That could include most elements of Trump’s 28-point plan without Ukraine’s withdrawal from the territory it currently controls. This would allow Putin to build a relationship with the United States in the time Trump has left as president—removing sanctions, rejoining the G7, and trying to undermine the NATO alliance indirectly through a partnership with Trump.
For all of Trump’s bluster on Europe, he has real incentives to push back now to prevent a crisis that could spiral out of control. His administration has options to deter Putin, if it wants to use them. For instance, Washington could warn Moscow that if it continues its deniable attacks in Europe, the United States would support Ukrainian access to Starlink inside Russia, which would improve the effectiveness of Kyiv’s long-range strike campaign.
On his way to Moscow, Ratcliffe stopped in Latvia. Today, the Latvian prime minister called the trip a “very good signal,” which seemed to imply that Ratcliffe had been there seeking to bolster European security. If the CIA director carried a warning with him, it should have been an unambiguous one: Any attack on NATO territory would bring in the United States. Trump might not want to make that type of commitment, but it may be necessary to ensure that Putin never concludes that he has an opportunity to start a war that breaks NATO.

articles.title: Sửa Luật Phòng, chống tác hại thuốc lá: Lấp khoảng trống, siết thực thi
articles.text:
Tại tọa đàm "Góp ý Dự thảo Luật Phòng, chống tác hại của thuốc lá (PCTHTL)(sửa đổi): Tăng cường hiệu quả thực thi và phối hợp liên ngành" do Báo Tiền Phong tổ chức ngày 26/8, TS.BS Dương Huy Lương, Phó Cục trưởng Cục Quản lý Khám, chữa bệnh, Bộ Y Tế cho hay, lần sửa Luật Phòng, chống tác hại của thuốc lá cần xây dựng một khung pháp lý có tính bao quát và dự báo. Chúng ta mong muốn xây dựng một đạo luật tiệm cận các quy định của thế giới, đặt ưu tiên cao nhất là bảo vệ sức khỏe người tiêu dùng, thế hệ trẻ và xã hội. Nhưng đồng thời, đây cũng là vấn đề của sản xuất, tiêu dùng, kinh tế và xã hội, đòi hỏi phải hài hòa lợi ích của Nhà nước, doanh nghiệp và các thành phần khác.
"Bộ Y tế cần có đầy đủ dữ liệu và phối hợp rất chặt chẽ với các bộ, ngành để tạo ra hành lang, khung pháp lý phù hợp, không chỉ phục vụ mục tiêu phòng, chống tác hại của thuốc lá mà còn bảo đảm các ngành, lĩnh vực khác không bị ách tắc bởi những quy định của luật", ông Lương cho hay.
Theo ông Lương, mục tiêu của Luật Phòng, chống tác hại của thuốc lá không phải là "chống thuốc lá" một cách cực đoan, mà là phòng ngừa, kiểm soát những tác hại của thuốc lá đối với sức khỏe con người. Về nguyên tắc, những doanh nghiệp đã được cấp phép vẫn được hoạt động trong thời hạn giấy phép. Tuy nhiên, xu hướng chung của ngành thuốc lá trong nước và thế giới cần chuyển dịch theo hướng giảm tác hại đối với sức khỏe.
Đóng góp ý kiến tại tọa đàm, các đại biểu nhấn mạnh yêu cầu tiếp tục rà soát, hoàn thiện Dự thảo Luật sửa đổi, bổ sung một số điều của Luật Phòng, chống tác hại của thuốc lá nhằm bảo đảm tính hợp hiến, hợp pháp, tính thống nhất của hệ thống pháp luật và tính khả thi khi triển khai trên thực tế. Đồng thời, tập trung vào việc tiếp tục rà soát tính phù hợp của một số quy định trong dự thảo với Nghị quyết số 173/2024/QH15 của Quốc hội. Theo đó, các khái niệm về thuốc lá điện tử, thuốc lá nung nóng và các sản phẩm thuốc lá khác cần được hoàn thiện nhằm bảo đảm cơ sở pháp lý và kỹ thuật rõ ràng cho quá trình áp dụng trên thực tế.
Bên cạnh đó, nhiều ý kiến đề nghị tiếp tục rà soát tính thống nhất của dự thảo với các luật có liên quan, đặc biệt là Luật Đầu tư 2025 và các văn bản liên quan.
Các đại biểu đồng thời nhấn mạnh sự cần thiết của cơ chế theo dõi, đánh giá và rà soát định kỳ sau khi chính sách được ban hành. Việc dựa trên dữ liệu thực tiễn và các chỉ số đo lường cụ thể sẽ giúp kịp thời nhận diện những thay đổi về hành vi tiêu dùng, diễn biến thị trường và các vấn đề phát sinh, từ đó có những điều chỉnh phù hợp nhằm bảo đảm hiệu quả lâu dài của chính sách.
Góp ý cho dự thảo luật, ông Nguyễn Chí Nhân, Tổng Thư ký Hiệp hội Thuốc lá Việt Nam cho rằng, Hiệp hội ủng hộ các quy định chặt chẽ trong dự thảo Luật sửa đổi, bổ sung một số điều của Luật Phòng, chống tác hại của thuốc lá, trong đó có đề xuất cấm thuốc lá điện tử, thuốc lá thế hệ mới và cấm trưng bày thuốc lá tại điểm bán. Tuy nhiên, đại diện Hiệp hội cho rằng cần tính toán kỹ khả năng thực thi và cách định nghĩa để tránh phát sinh khoảng trống pháp lý.
Từ góc độ lập pháp, bà Nguyễn Quỳnh Liên, Đại biểu Quốc hội hoạt động chuyên trách tại Ủy ban Pháp luật và Tư pháp của Quốc hội, nguyên Trưởng Ban Dân chủ, Giám sát và Phản biện xã hội, Ủy ban Trung ương MTTQ Việt Nam cho rằng, hiệu quả thực thi cần được đặt ở trung tâm của quá trình sửa đổi Luật. Nghị quyết 173 mới dừng ở việc xác định khái niệm, trong khi Luật sửa đổi cần làm rõ cụ thể những sản phẩm nào bị cấm, đồng thời tính đến toàn bộ chuỗi từ sản xuất, kinh doanh đến nhập khẩu và lưu thông. Đây không chỉ là vấn đề quy định trong Luật mà còn phải gắn chặt với tính khả thi và hiệu quả thực thi; chính sách cần xác định rõ sản phẩm nào được phép lưu hành, đi kèm các tiêu chuẩn và biện pháp kiểm soát tác hại, cũng như các quy định minh bạch để cơ quan quản lý có cơ sở cấp phép, thanh tra và xử lý vi phạm...

articles.title: Gã trai trẻ khai chỉ cần mặc đẹp, lái xe sang là nữ đại gia móc hầu bao 14 tỷ đồng
articles.text:
Lập công ty, lôi kéo nhân viên tham gia lừa đảo
Ngày 26/8, Tòa án nhân dân thành phố Hà Nội tuyên phạt bị cáo Lương Văn Quỳnh (SN 2000, ở Bắc Ninh) mức án 9 năm tù và Nguyễn Văn Sùng (SN 2003, ở Bắc Ninh) mức án 7 năm tù về tội “Lừa đảo chiếm đoạt tài sản”.
Hai bị cáo bị xác định phạm tội trong đường dây “đóng vai người thành đạt” để lôi kéo đầu tư tài chính, ngoại hối, để chiếm đoạt hơn 40 tỷ đồng, do đối tượng Hồ Bích Ngọc (SN 1996, ở Hà Nội) cầm đầu.
Trước đó đầu tháng 2/2026, Hồ Bích Ngọc đã bị Tòa án nhân dân thành phố Hà Nội xét xử, tuyên án 13 năm tù về tội “Lừa đảo chiếm đoạt tài sản” và “Cho vay lãi nặng trong giao dịch dân sự”. 35 đồng phạm khác của Ngọc cũng phải nhận các mức án tương xứng với tội danh.
Theo cáo trạng, hoạt động đầu tư ngoại hối trên các sàn giao dịch chứng khoán quốc tế trực tuyến chưa được pháp luật Việt Nam công nhận. Tuy nhiên, tại Việt Nam, các nhà đầu tư vẫn tham gia giao dịch, đầu tư vào sàn.
Năm 2019, Hồ Bích Ngọc làm Sale cho một văn phòng giao dịch ngoại hối Forex nên nắm được một vài “mánh khóe”. Đến năm 2020, Ngọc thành lập Công ty Trách nhiệm hữu hạn Thương mại và Tư vấn Đầu tư Master Group.
Công ty dù không được cấp phép nhưng Ngọc vẫn điều hành nhân viên hoạt động trong lĩnh vực tư vấn đầu tư tài chính, ngoại hối, nhằm mục đích lôi kéo khách hàng tham gia đầu tư để chiếm đoạt tài sản.
Ngọc quen biết các đối tượng tên “Peter” và “Alex” qua Telegram, trong đó Peter giới thiệu là đại diện của 2 sàn GFS và TOPMAX; còn “Alex” là đại diện sàn Richsmart.
Quá trình trao đổi, Ngọc nhận làm “Referral link” (tức làm liên kết giới thiệu) cho các sàn giao dịch ngoại hối trên.
Chỉ cần làm 'bóng' hình thức bề ngoài là bị hại sập bẫy
Theo đó, Ngọc liên hệ với bộ phận hỗ trợ (Support) của các sàn giao dịch này thông qua Email hoặc “Chat bot” trên sàn giao dịch để được cấp “tài khoản môi giới” (Link ref) để hoạt động. Sau đó, Ngọc sẽ được trả tiền hoa hồng môi giới theo khối lượng giao dịch của đối tác gắn với tài khoản, đó gọi là tiền COM.
Ngọc thỏa thuận về hoa hồng môi giới với các sàn và yêu cầu bộ phận hỗ trợ của sàn cài đặt tiền hoa hồng theo cấp độ 1, 2, 3, 4 để Ngọc cài cho các tài khoản cấp dưới, gồm: Cấp Quản lý, Leader, Sale, Khách hàng được Back COM. Tổng tiền hoa hồng Ngọc nhận được sẽ chia cho các “tài khoản môi giới” phía dưới.
Hai bị cáo Quỳnh và Sùng, bị cáo buộc làm trong đường dây của Ngọc. Cả hai đều là trưởng nhóm (Leader), đã thực hiện nhiều vụ lừa đảo chiếm đoạt tài sản của các bị hại.
Trong đó, bị cáo Lương Văn Quỳnh đã trực tiếp thực hiện 3 vụ lừa đảo, chiếm đoạt tổng số hơn 19 tỷ đồng, hưởng lợi bất chính hơn 440 triệu đồng; Nguyễn Văn Sùng thực hiện một vụ lừa đảo chiếm đoạt 1 tỷ đồng, hưởng lợi hơn 144 triệu đồng.
Sau khi vụ án bị phát hiện Quỳnh và Sùng bỏ trốn, bị truy nã, đến tháng 2/2026, cả hai ra đầu thú.
Tại tòa, bị cáo Quỳnh khai mỗi lần đi gặp khách hàng anh ta mượn xe sang của Ngọc để “làm màu”. Trong lần đi gặp một nữ đại gia, Quỳnh lái chiếc Mercedes đã khiến nữ đại gia "xuống tiền" đầu tư, rồi bị chiếm đoạt 14 tỷ đồng.
Quỳnh cho biết, chỉ việc ăn mặc đẹp, đi xe sang, uống cà phê và mời khách đầu tư. Cứ có khách là bị cáo được hưởng tiền và khi bị hại bỏ nhiều tiền vào sàn, thì sàn lập tức bị đánh “sập”.

articles.title: The Lights Are Back On in Gary, Indiana
articles.text:
The Lights Are Back On in Gary, Indiana
A long two weeks after a derecho blew through, most of the city finally has power.
 
 Last night, NIPSCO, an Indiana utility company that provides electricity to half a million people in the northern part of the state, finally made the deadline for restoring power to the city of Gary. On August 11, a derecho swept across northwest Indiana, and winds nearing 100 miles an hour knocked out power for more than 370,000 people, NIPSCO has said. In Gary, home to nearly 70,000 people, 75 percent of them Black, more than half of the utility’s customers lost power in the initial aftermath of the storm. For the next two weeks, NIPSCO kept pushing back its timeline for restoring power; even on Monday, thousands in Gary were still in the dark. As of yesterday evening, the utility said, it had restored power to 99 percent of its customers—which also meant that hundreds of people in Gary still didn’t have electricity this morning.
Blackouts follow plenty of storms, and at a press conference eight days after the storm hit, Gary Mayor Eddie Melton described the ongoing blackout as a situation for “not just Gary” but also all of northwest Indiana. However, as the days of darkness stretched on, and the power started going back in other parts of the region—first Dyer and East Chicago, then Hobart and Merrillville—the initial inconvenience of a Tuesday, a Wednesday, then a Thursday, then a Friday without power started to become a crisis in Gary. This past weekend, Melton was no longer talking about the blackout as a regional problem. Gary, he told me, had not initially been on NIPSCO’s schedule for restoring power and had seemingly been overlooked until the city pushed back.
NIPSCO declined to comment on the specifics of its restoration schedule, but a spokesperson wrote in a statement that it had hired extra contractors and drawn on support from neighboring utilities and that “no outage is being overlooked.”
 
 The people I spoke with in Gary felt differently—that whatever efforts had been made to restore power had not been fast enough. They described throwing out maggot-filled food from their refrigerators, and temporarily moving in with friends and family members who had generators. They were charging their phones in their cars while running the air-conditioning just to stay cool in the summer heat. Gary’s median household income is about $40,000 a year; nearly 20 percent of its people are 65 or older, according to the latest U.S. census data—it’s a community with limited money to spare. People were spending their last dollars on gas to drive through the city on roads without functional streetlights—past uprooted trees, fallen street signs, and loose power lines—just to find supplies.
As the power outage dragged on, relief efforts started reaching the city, but some were first come, first served; others limited relief packages to one per household, which kept people from picking up extra care packages for neighbors stuck at home. “Our seniors are stuck in their apartments, completely dark,” Willett Wright, a 77-year-old resident who was still without power, told me. “There’s no generators in the world that can get up to their apartments. They’re stuck in their rooms with all this heat, and no food.”
 Power slowly began to come back this weekend, but not across all of Gary’s neighborhoods. Some residents were still waiting in the dark. And even in the places where power had come back on, the lights were still flickering. If you ask Gary residents what time their power was turned back on, they can share it almost down to the minute: 11:32 p.m. on Saturday; just after midnight on Sunday; 2:45 p.m. on Monday.
 Indiana is used to dealing with some types of severe storms, which were responsible for nearly 50 percent of the major disaster costs in the state over the past 44 years, a 2025 report from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration found. But this derecho—a strong windstorm that moves in straight lines and can be as fast as a hurricane or a tornado—felt different, residents told me. Climate change is contributing to a steady increase in storm frequency and severity across the United States, which is in turn increasing damage to power grids across the country, Kyri Baker, a University of Colorado at Boulder associate professor who focuses on power systems and power-grid resilience, told me. “A lot of the extreme weather events are happening in areas that we didn’t initially expect,” she said. “Utilities need to change their game plans in preparing for those low-probability events.”
Gary’s problems with infrastructure were clear long before the storm rolled in. Over the past decades, as deindustrialization has shrunk the city’s population and tax base, its infrastructure has crumbled too. NIPSCO has a monopoly on Gary’s electricity, and a 2025 analysis by the Citizens Action Coalition, a consumer-advocacy organization, found that NIPSCO customers were already paying the highest bills of any of Indiana’s five investor-owned electric utilities; last year, NIPSCO was approved for another rate increase to upgrade power lines and technology updates. Even though low-income Black households tend to spend more of their incomes on utilities, they are disproportionately affected by electric-grid failures and face slower restoration times after extreme weather events. (NIPSCO did not respond to questions about its infrastructure investments or its rates.)
 Each day that the lights stayed off added to the disruption in people’s lives. David Rucker and his wife, Tiffany, told me that they’d had to drive about an hour every day to Chicago to charge his BiPAP ventilator, which he needs to breathe when he sleeps. The device runs only four hours when it’s battery-powered. Although Gary is only about 30 minutes away from the south side of Chicago, the journey takes twice as long, because their car’s transmission needs to be fixed. “The money we would’ve spent to fix it, we don’t have,” Tiffany said. “Now everything is depleted. The storm has taken a lot—mentally, physically, and monetarily.” Their power was restored on Monday night at 10 p.m.
As the power comes back on, people are ready to restock and return to a sense of normalcy. They are refilling insulin prescriptions that went bad in warm refrigerators, recharging glucometers, and getting wellness check-ups for high blood pressure and A1C levels, practitioners at Gary’s NorthShore Health Center said. Several people I spoke with said that they are cautiously refilling their refrigerators with groceries, and stocking up on batteries in case of another emergency. Earlier this week, Indiana Governor Mike Braun requested an investigation into NIPSCO’s tree maintenance, as well as a review of approved state funds for the city’s infrastructure. Yesterday, President Trump approved a major-disaster declaration for Indiana, allowing FEMA aid to help the state recover from the damage. The city is finally getting some of the attention and help it has long needed.

articles.title: What Are Jewish Voters Supposed to Do?
articles.text:
What Are Jewish Voters Supposed to Do?
Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel on why she is skipping the Michigan Democratic Party’s convention, the rise of anti-Semitism within her party, and the conundrum Jewish Democrat voters face. Plus: a new round of President Trump’s Canadian trade war, and American Scoundrel, by Kai Bird and Susan Goldmark.
Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube
On this week’s episode of The David Frum Show, The Atlantic’s David Frum opens with his thoughts on the blowing up of trade talks between the United States and Canada, and President Trump’s reckless trade war against Canada. David discusses how this trade war hurts not only America’s relationship with Canada but its global standing as a reliable trade partner.
Then David is joined by Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel to discuss the growing hostility among some Democratic voters toward American Jews. Frum and Nessel discuss why the rhetoric of Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed concerns some Jews; rise of anti-Semitism within the Democratic party; and the impossible situation many Jewish voters find themselves in today.
Finally, David ends the show with his thoughts on the new biography on Roy Cohn, American Scoundrel.
The following is a transcript of the episode:
Dana Nessel: I think it’s a fundamental mistake for the Democratic Party to think that you can just push Jewish Democrats out and simply replace them with any other population.
[Music]
David Frum: Welcome to The David Frum Show. I’m David Frum, a staff writer at The Atlantic. My guest this week will be Dana Nessel, attorney general of the state of Michigan, and this week’s book will be the newly released biography American Scoundrel, a biography of Roy Cohn and his lifetime from Joe McCarthy to Donald Trump. Before either the dialogue with Attorney General Nessel or the book, I want to open with some thoughts about the recent blowup in trade negotiations between the United States and Canada.
Now, it’s the Trump administration, though, so those negotiations are blown up as I record on Monday, August 24th. They may be back on by the time you watch on Wednesday, August 26th. Anything can happen with this crazy crew. But let’s assume, as I record, that the negotiations remain blown up for some time.
Now, I wrote in The Atlantic this past weekend an analysis of the economic effect of the blowup of these negotiations, and I hope you’ll take a look at that. Facts, figures, dates, numbers. What I want to talk about today is not the economics—you can read that in The Atlantic, and I hope you will. What I want to talk about is some of the geopolitical implications of the United States behaving in the predatory way that the Trump administration has led the United States to behave in these negotiations with Canada.
Look, I’m recording this in Canada right now as I speak. I do have a Canadian point of view. But I think I can speak more broadly when I say that America has enormously benefited all around the world in reputation and standing from its relationship with Canada.
The U.S.-Canada relationship is a kind of text proof of America’s benignity and good intentions. If you’re a country anywhere in the world, wondering whether to partner with the United States or one of its adversaries—the Soviet Union in the olden days, Russia or China now—you’d look at the U.S.-Canada relationship and say, There is America’s nearest neighbor, a country only one-tenth the size of the United States—smaller in economics, smaller in population—highly vulnerable to American pressure, and yet America has consistently treated Canada as an equal, as a partner, and as a friend. And that model relationship is a proof of the good intentions of America to anybody. And so there you are on the other side of the world thinking, Can we trust the Americans? Think, Well, the Canadians next door; they trust the Americans. They’ve benefited from that trust. They’ve been treated with equality. So will we. So long as the relationship worked, America stood proud in the eyes of the world.
The Trump vision of America is very different. At home, Trump’s vision of how America should arrange its economy borrows a lot from China. As much as Trump rails against China, he wants America to be more like China. His government is taking ownership stakes in major corporations. Favors are dispensed according to cronyism and patronage. He attempts to intervene in the courts on behalf of his own interests in a way that [is] very familiar to those who follow the horrible precedents of the Chinese Communist Party. And internationally, his foreign policy looks not like America as we knew it—the world leader of a coalition of democratic states bound by agreements and treaties negotiated in good faith—but like Russia, a country that has given up on the rest of the world in order to be a bully and hegemon at home.
I think a lot of Canadians feel that what Trump wants from these trade negotiations is not actually any kind of deal. He wants to turn Canada into a kind of American Belarus—a satellite state, nominally independent, but in fact governed from the capital, that can be dominated to create a larger imperial zone where the imperial power does its economics not by trade and mutual benefit, but by domination, predation, and exploitation.
If you’re a country on the other side of the world without a long, friendly history with the United States, if you’re an Indonesia, if you’re a Malaysia, if you’re a Philippines, if you’re a Vietnam, and you look at what Trump is doing to Canada, you think, What will they do to me? We don’t share a language with the Americans. We were not their allies in two world wars. If they will do that to their nearest neighbor and closest partner, what will they do to us? And it sends a message to the whole planet that America is reinventing itself—not as the leader of a league of democracies, but as an imperial power. Much like other imperial powers, much like Russia, much like China. Corrupt at home, dominant abroad, and maybe somebody you have to deal with because they’re so big and rich and powerful, but not someone you want to be a partner with. Certainly not someone you can trust.
The message to the world from the blowup of U.S.-Canada relations is: Look, the Canadians, they’ve got the geography they’ve got. They have very few options. Ditto Mexico. But we? We’re farther away. We have options. And what would be wise for us is to keep an equal distance between the United States and China as we keep an equal distance between the United States and Russia, because what Trump is proving to us again and again is that America is no different and no better than those other powers.
That’s one of Donald Trump’s big ideas. He’s said often in interviews, even when he was running for president and in his first term, Do you think we’re any different from anybody else? He really doesn’t believe America’s different from anybody else, and he’s led America to behave in ways that are no different from anybody else.
But, you know, one of the things that Canadians have kept alive through all these dark months is a confidence that the Americans really are different from everybody else—and that the past of the American-Canadian relationship, that’s the truth. And it’s the present that is the dead end and the false start and the misdirection. So what we all try to keep alive here—and I speak to you from the north shore of Lake Ontario, from a road named for the losers of the American Revolution, Loyalist Parkway—the faith that is kept alive here is a faith that there’s a better America, and maybe someday it will rediscover itself. I hope that’s a faith that Americans can rediscover, too, and hold onto, too, through some very dark chapters.
And now my dialogue with Attorney General Dana Nessel.
[Music]
Frum: Dana Nessel has spent the past eight years as Michigan’s attorney general. She built her career litigating civil-rights cases before winning the attorney general’s office in 2018. In office, she closed an investigation into Michigan State University’s handling of the Larry Nassar sexual-abuse scandal, led the state prosecution of the men who plotted to kidnap Michigan Governor Gretchen Whitmer, and brought charges against 16 Republicans who falsely certified Trump as Michigan’s 2020 election winner.
Term-limited out of office this January, Nessel has become an important voice in debates over the future of the Democratic Party of Michigan, and especially against the anti-Semitism she sees rising within it.
She was born in West Bloomfield Township: the site of the March 12th, 2026, terror attack on Temple Israel, the nation’s largest Reform synagogue, and a preschool with 140 children inside.
Attorney General Nessel, thank you for joining me today.
Nessel: Thanks for having me.
Frum: Let’s start, if we may, by just talking a little bit about your personal experiences as a Jewish Democrat in Michigan. You have said that you have felt unsafe attending your own party’s state convention. Tell us what it has been like this summer for you.
Nessel: Well, look, it’s been difficult, candidly, since I entered office, and it’s strange because I sort of built my career prior to becoming attorney general on being an advocate for LGBTQ rights and being very involved in the marriage-equality case that ultimately was resolved by the United States Supreme Court. And this has been my focus for much of the time. Yes, I’m also Jewish, but I’m a gay person in a same-sex marriage, and I had really thought coming into office that was what would make me stand out or be unusual as the first openly gay person to serve in statewide office in Michigan. But that’s not really been my experience, and in fact, since I’ve been in office, it’s been much more interesting to people that I’m actually the first Jewish attorney general in Michigan history. And I would say that, again, I have been bombarded with death threats since the first days that I took office. And at any given time normally, there’s about three people who are currently either serving a sentence in state or federal prison or on probation or somewhere in the proceedings for anti-Semitic death threats against me.
So that was a surprise to me. But things changed in so many different ways after October 7th. And then it wasn’t just, basically, I would say mentally unstable people on the far right that were threatening me or other Jews, but now it became really a both-sides situation, and I began to perceive an enormous amount of anti-Semitism within the Democratic Party.
And so it’s been a challenge since that time, and it’s gotten worse and worse. And what I am seeing from, again, people that I know in my party [is] a fundamental lack of knowledge about Judaism, about my religion, as well as about sort of the historical aspects of the state of Israel and also a complete ignorance about what ties Jews around the globe to Israel itself. And I think that’s really caused a rise in, again, they would call it anti-Zionism, but I call it anti-Semitism.
Frum: Let’s talk a little bit about the reaction or the aftermath of this dreadful attack, attempted attack, on Temple Israel this year. It would’ve targeted children above all—potentially as many as 140 school-aged children. That’s your town, as I said in the introduction. What has it been like to be in a state where such a thing could happen, and how has the reaction to that terrible attempt lived up to, or not lived up to, your hopes and expectations for your state?
Nessel: Well, first of all, I learned about what was happening at Temple Israel from my own son, who was at my parents’ house, that’s just down the street from Temple Israel. And so it was close enough that you could hear all the sirens and all the commotion going on. And I have many members of my family that have been longtime members of Temple Israel. It’s really a focal point of the Jewish community, because it is the biggest Reform temple anywhere in the world.
But, you know, the reaction to it—obviously there’s a lot of people who were quick to call this out. But, you know, I think most concerning, of course, was the statement that our nominee for U.S. Senate made, which was that “hurt people hurt people.” And a lot of us perceived that as sort of making excuses for somebody who sought to murder over 100 pre-K schoolchildren. And that’s the kind of mentality that bothers me a lot.
I will tell you that in 2019, very early on in my tenure, you had that attack in New Zealand—the Christchurch attack that killed over 50 Muslims who were in the process of their congregation and praying. And I immediately went to one of the mosques in Dearborn, and I donned a hijab to be respectful, and I talked about Islamophobia and said it was unacceptable in any realm for any reason. And I didn’t try to get into, like, what were the motivations of the person who killed these people, and did he have mental-health issues? Did he have bad experiences with Muslims? I just condemned it unequivocally, and I think that’s what people should have done with Temple Israel. You can’t make excuses for that kind of domestic terrorism.
Frum: Well, since you’ve raised the Democratic nominee, let me go through the timeline of his statements, so we get a sense of what is fair to say about those statements and what is not. The attempt happened, as you say, on March the 12th of this year. It was heroically averted, and the gunman was deservedly the only casualty, or the would-be gunman. On March 12th, Abdul El-Sayed, who was not yet then the nominee, released a statement that said, “I was horrified and heartbroken this afternoon to hear the reports of an active shooter at Temple Israel in West Bloomfield. I’m thankful that no worshippers, students, or teachers were harmed. We all owe a debt of gratitude to Temple security and law enforcement, who acted swiftly to keep the community safe. To my Jewish sisters and brothers, you have a right to worship in peace … there is no room for antisemitism in America.” So that’s good. That was a statement written by who knows who.
The next day, Abdul El-Sayed released a video with his own face and his own voice, and there he said, “Yesterday, our state was rocked by news of a heinous attack on Temple Israel … I grew up not 15 minutes away from Temple Israel. Many of my childhood friends and classmates worship there.” Good start. But then he goes on to say, “A week earlier, an airstrike killed the niece and nephew of the gunman. Imagine if that had never happened. Imagine there was no war in Iran. Imagine if there were no airstrikes in Lebanon. Imagine if his family had never died. We can and must condemn the attack on Temple Israel, and we can and must condemn the violence 6,000 miles away.” So that’s not so good.
And then on March 18th, on an internal call, which became public via Punchbowl News, El-Sayed acknowledged that the statement he had made in his own voice and face was a risk, but said he was proud to take the risk.
And on March 24th, 25th, speaking on Twitter or X, he said, “I called out the antisemitic attack on Temple Israel immediately. The risk I took that these cowards will never take is having the courage to call out an illegal and unjustified war that’s killing children, wasting our tax dollars, and spiking gas prices, too.”
So, he himself had made clear that when he took a risk, the risk was the equation of two completely different things in completely different contexts. So if you’re a Jewish person, I think you hear that, or a friend of the Jews, or someone who cares about Jews, or just a person who cares about condemning terrorism, it sounds like, you know: I’m not making excuses, but I have an excuse.
Nessel: Yeah. So I will say this. Since Abdul’s win, during the course of the primary, this has been a conversation that has continued with the Jewish community, not exclusively, but most of whom supported Haley Stevens. And you know, Abdul has been going through the process, to his credit, of having meetings with Michigan Jewish electeds and the Michigan Jewish caucus of the Michigan Democratic Party. And I think privately, he will say that he regrets having made those remarks. But here we are, it’s almost the end of of August, and he still has not withdrawn those statements and said, I misspoke, or, I now recognize the harm that I caused by making those statements. And it has me concerned that he really stands by them.
And if so, what does that mean for American Jews moving forward if you can rationalize what’s happening in a war in the Middle East on attacks on your own people here in the state of Michigan? That is deeply concerning to me, and I think by the same logic you would say, if Iran were to attack, whether it would be a government building or a church or a mall or what have you, that we would just deserve those attacks because, of course, we are engaged in this war in Iran. And really the list goes on and on, as to how you could make excuses for acts of domestic terrorism.
I don’t think we should ever be making those kinds of excuses, and in a way, propping up people who maybe seek to commit those crimes. It’s a dangerous, dangerous world to live in where you have somebody who supports that kind of logic.
Frum: Well, every terrorist, every killer has a reason. I mean, except for the ones who are so divorced from reality that they operate in a world that is impenetrable to anybody’s reason. But most of them have some kind of professed grievance, some kind of reason, some kind of ideology, some kind of motive. So would you explain, just because some people may have difficulty with this—walk us through this as a prosecutor, as a lawyer. What is wrong with, after you say, I condemn this attack on the Black church, on the mosque, on the Jewish pre- preschool, then going to say: However, I do understand why the killer acted the way he did. What is wrong with that?
Nessel: Well, obviously, when you are providing some sort of rational explanation for why it occurs, I think it possibly encourages other people to do the same. They want to be a hero, too. And that’s why I think we have to have unequivocal condemnation of those kinds of acts.
And, you know, we’ve had many mass-casualty episodes in Michigan just recently. We had a man who killed his entire family. He had been going through a difficult divorce, but I wouldn’t say that’s a good excuse for having murdered his entire family. We’ve had many other events, right? We had a shooting at Michigan State University. We had a shooting at Oxford High School. Many people died during the course of those events, but I don’t recall something similar where people were like, Well, let’s understand the killer’s mental-health concerns or issues that they were going through so that we can better understand a rationale for him doing that. We just, we condemn it.
Frum: Well, correct me if I have this wrong, but my understanding is that the attempted killer in West Bloomfield was not mentally unstable, did not have mental-health issues. He had a cause; he had a grievance. He had come to the United States from another country. He had a political ideology. He had affiliations in that other country. He amassed a considerable arsenal of weapons, and he chose his target very carefully to make a political point. So it’s not a question of mental health; it’s a question of political ideology, which expressed itself through the attempted killing of hundreds of, or dozens of, schoolchildren.
So when you talk about it, I think it’s true—if you had somebody who really was wildly mentally unstable, and they committed a crime that cost human life, it might not be inappropriate to say, This person was mentally unstable, and that’s why they did it. But that’s not what seems to happen here. This seems to be, you’re not endorsing—you’re not trying to spread understanding of the need for greater attention to mental health. You’re drawing attention to a cause that you think somehow balances the scales.
Nessel: I mean, I’m not going to try to excuse the statements that Abdul made in regard to that. And in fact many of us have been outspoken against it. I still—I leave hope for the fact that Abdul will have heard what many of us have said about why we’re very upset about those remarks. And that he will seek to, I don’t want to say clarify, but at least to withdraw those earlier remarks, because he now has a greater understanding of it. That’s my hope, and I’ve had that conversation with him personally. He still hasn’t done it, but I hope that we’ll hear more from him about this soon.
Frum: Well, you’ve spent your life in public office. You’ve won election to high statewide office. How much comfort do you take if—you remember the famous line from the movie, Damn right, I ordered the code red? And weeks or months after the person has said, Damn right, I ordered the code red, and the anti-code-red coalition mobilizes votes against him, says, On second thought, I misspoke when I ordered the code red, now that I realize how much harm I did. Maybe the first statement is the authentic one, and the later one is not to be taken so seriously?
Nessel: Yeah. Well, what I’d like to hear, obviously, from him is that he understands now why those statements are so harmful, and why he shouldn’t be making any kinds of excuses or rationalizations. I mean, people can evolve, and people can be educated, and that’s one of the things that I’ve said to him, and other Jewish electeds or leaders of the community have tried to convey to him.
I mean, there are certainly things that I have said in the past where I displayed some kind of ignorance about an issue, and then you had stakeholders come to me and say, Hey, what you said is offensive to us. Let us tell you why. And I can say, Oh, my gosh, I never looked at it from that perspective, and I now understand, and I will never say anything like that again.
I have done that. So I think that Abdul could also do that, obviously, you know? I mean, obviously there’s more issues than just this one statement about what happened at Temple Israel.
